name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell

lines.s10: Mourvèdre is the dark, meaty red of Bandol on the Provence coast, blackberry and leather on a firm grip, known in Spain as Monastrell.
lines.s20: Mourvèdre is a late ripening black grape that needs real heat, at home in Bandol and, as Monastrell, in south eastern Spain. It gives blackberry, black plum and a gamey, leathery depth, with firm tannin that asks for food or for time.
lines.s45: Mourvèdre ripens very late, so it only thrives where the summer is long and hot. Its French home is Bandol, on the Provence coast, and Spain, where it began, calls it Monastrell. It is nearly black, tasting of blackberry and black plum, with leather and a gamey, meaty note. It is full bodied, with a firm, drying grip. Bandol ages it at least eighteen months in wood, and tends to be sterner than the riper wines of Spain, California or Australia. Pour it with braised lamb, grilled sausages or game. Bandol growers say it wants its head in the sun and its feet in the water.
lines.sale: Mourvèdre is the bottle for a table that likes its red dark and a little wild: blackberry, leather and a gamey depth. Have it with the lamb or the game, and give it time in the glass.

glass.lead: Blackberry and black plum under leather, black pepper and a gamey, meaty depth, nearly black, full and firmly tannic.

ladder.where: Bandol, where the sea tempers the heat
Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante, the Barossa and Paso Robles

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin high and gripping, alcohol medium plus to high, body full.

old.where: Bandol and the southern Rhône; Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante as Monastrell
old.glass: Bandol tends to be stern and savoury: blackberry and black plum under leather, game, dried thyme and black pepper, with high, gripping tannin that needs years. Spanish Monastrell is usually riper, with blackberry jam, dried fig and higher alcohol.
old.cellar: Bandol red is at least half Mourvèdre, with Grenache and Cinsault, and spends eighteen months or more in wood, by tradition large old casks.

new.where: Barossa and McLaren Vale as Mataro; Contra Costa and Paso Robles; Washington
new.glass: Typically riper and fuller in fruit: blackberry and black plum with dark chocolate and liquorice, at higher alcohol, the meaty note there but less to the fore. On a list it is most often the third grape of a GSM.
new.cellar: Mostly blended with Grenache and Shiraz or Syrah; a few wines from very old vines are bottled alone, as Mataro or Mourvèdre.

contrast.why: Mourvèdre ripens very late, so both worlds plant it in heat. Bandol's law asks for a high share of the grape and long ageing in wood, hence firm wines for keeping. Elsewhere it is picked riper and mostly blended.
contrast.blur: Jumilla sits in the Old World yet gives ripe, sweet fruited Monastrell, and old vine wines from Contra Costa or the Barossa can be as firm and gamey as Bandol.
contrast.call: Dried thyme, leather and a stern grip with fresher fruit lean Bandol; blackberry jam, dried fig and higher alcohol lean Spain or the New World.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; Bandol rosé cold, as a white.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass for the red; a white wine glass for Bandol rosé.
service.decant: Consider it for a young Bandol after tasting a sample; air can lift a closed, gamey first scent.
service.age: Bandol rewards ten years and more; most Monastrell and New World blends are ready within five.

with.why: richness and long cooking to match the grip
the wine's own gamey note meets the meat
fat and salt ease the firm tannin
a rosé with the weight for mustard and paprika

labels.means: The grape's Spanish name, on wines from Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante.
The old name in Australia and California; many labels there now say Mourvèdre.
A Provence place name: the red is at least half Mourvèdre, and the rosé holds it too.
Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre: in the blend Mourvèdre brings colour, grip and a savoury depth.

guest.q: Why does this wine smell a little gamey?
guest.a: That is Mourvèdre. It often carries a meaty, leathery scent, strongest when the wine is young and closed, and a little air usually lets the blackberry come forward.

guest.q: Is Monastrell the same grape as Mourvèdre?
guest.a: Yes. Monastrell is its Spanish name, and Spain is where the grape began. Australia and California long called it Mataro.
No. Bandol is known for rosé, but its red is the serious one: at least half Mourvèdre, aged eighteen months in wood and made to keep for ten years or more.

compare.tell: Syrah is more polished and peppery, with violet and black olive; Mourvèdre is gamier and more rustic, with leather and a heavier grip.
Grenache is far paler and softer, with strawberry and kirsch; Mourvèdre is nearly black, with blackberry, leather and high tannin.
Carignan is higher in acidity, with cranberry and black raspberry; Mourvèdre is darker and meatier, with only medium acidity.

cards.front: Mourvèdre: its names in Spain and in Australia, and its French home?
cards.back: Monastrell in Spain; Mataro in Australia and California. Its French home is Bandol, on the Provence coast.

cards.front: Bandol red: how much Mourvèdre, and how long in wood?
cards.back: At least 50 per cent Mourvèdre, with Grenache and Cinsault, and at least eighteen months in wood, by tradition large old casks.

cards.front: Mourvèdre blind: Bandol or a riper origin, what tips it?
cards.back: Dried thyme, leather and a stern grip with fresher fruit lean Bandol. Blackberry jam, dried fig, chocolate and higher alcohol lean Jumilla or the New World.

questions.q: A guest who enjoys a ripe Barossa blend of Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro asks for the Mataro grape from the Old World, in a firmer, more savoury style made for keeping. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Bandol red is at least half Mourvèdre, the grape Australia calls Mataro, and is typically stern, savoury and long lived. Cornas is Syrah, Cahors is Malbec and Madiran is Tannat.

questions.q: A blind red is nearly black and full, with blackberry, leather, dried thyme and a gamey, meaty note, on high, gripping tannin and medium acidity. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Leather and game on a nearly black, heavily tannic wine point to Mourvèdre. Syrah would show more pepper and violet with a finer grip, Carignan has higher acidity and Grenache is far paler.

questions.q: A guest orders a Spanish red labelled Monastrell from Jumilla and asks what to expect in the glass. What do you tell him?
opts: Dark, ripe and full, with blackberry and firm tannin
Pale and light, with sour cherry and high acidity
Medium bodied, with cassis, cedar and green bell pepper
Light and gently sparkling, with strawberry and some sweetness
questions.exp: Monastrell is Mourvèdre, and in hot Jumilla it gives dark, ripe, full wines with firm tannin. A pale, tart wine or one of cassis and cedar describes other grapes.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. TASTE.world reads old, and the entry agrees: the Old World side carries both Bandol and Spanish Monastrell, and the honest blind call is Bandol against everything riper, which is how the call is written.
No GRID_SAY: say is moor-VED-ruh with moh-nah-STRELL, the Spanish form on labels. Mataro is given under the labels.

The ladder has two rungs and no cool one. Bandol stands as moderate only because the sea tempers a hot site; the Régionale row calls the grape's climate hot, and a checker may prefer to read both rungs as warm and warmer.

The Codex's records on Mourvèdre read true and nothing here departs from them. Bandol red at 50 per cent Mourvèdre or more with Grenache and Cinsault, eighteen months in wood and the names Monastrell and Mataro are the Codex's own reviewed facts.

The saying about the head in the sun and the feet in the water stands on several trade and French pages read through search; one page gives the sea in place of the water. The official Bandol site did not appear in search.

The share of Mourvèdre in Bandol rosé, given on two pages as 20 per cent at least, was not confirmed against the appellation's rule and is left out; the label line says only that the rosé holds the grape.

A Spanish origin stands on Wine Grapes and on the common view; pages differ between Valencia and Catalonia for the place, so no place is named. The names Murviedro and Mataró as the roots of Mourvèdre and Mataro were confirmed and left out for room.

The New World style, riper and more openly fruity with less leather and game, stands on trade tasting notes of Barossa and Contra Costa wines read through search, not on a wine body's statement of style; the Barossa vineyard of 1853 was confirmed and is not named.
The Creole dish is shrimp remoulade with Bandol rosé, not the red: the Codex's own pairing notes offer Bandol rosé beside a mustard dish.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
